messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 38
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Fisherman
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 76

Adwoa is thirty-eight years old, a wife and mother of two, and a fisherman on Lake Volta in Ghana. She has been fishing since she was a girl, learning from her father. Now she works alongside her husband, Kofi, on their small wooden canoe. Every morning before dawn they push out onto the dark water, the only sound the dip of paddles and the low chatter of other boats. For years this was the rhythm of her life—hard, steady, familiar.

That rhythm shattered six months ago.

It was a quiet morning like any other. The net was heavy, tangled, and Kofi leaned far over the side to free it. Adwoa was at the stern, balancing the boat. She remembers the sudden list, the water rushing over the gunwale, and the way Kofi looked back at her with surprise—not fear, just surprise—before the canoe tipped. She grabbed the side, went under, came up gasping. The boat floated upside down. Kofi was not there. She screamed his name, paddled wildly, dove again and again until her lungs burned. Another fisherman pulled her into his boat. They found Kofi's body an hour later, tangled in the net that had become his shroud.

Now Adwoa still goes out on the lake. She has no choice. There are school fees to pay, children to feed. But everything has changed. She cannot stand near the edge of the canoe. She sits in the center, knees drawn up, hands gripping the wooden seat until her knuckles blanch. If the boat rocks even slightly—a shift of weight, a wave from a passing motor—her heart slams against her ribs and she starts to tremble. She cannot look down at the water. The green-black depth seems to pull at her, a heavy hunger. She focuses on the sky, on the far shore, on anything solid.

At night she does not sleep. She lies next to her mother-in-law's sleeping mat (she cannot bear the empty room she shared with Kofi) and listens to the crickets. When she finally drifts, she dreams of the net, of his face underwater, of her own hands reaching for nothing. She wakes drenched in sweat, the sheet twisted around her legs like rope. Sometimes she thinks she hears him calling her name across the water, but when she listens there is only the wind.

Her daughter, eight-year-old Ama, tries to help. "Mama, I will paddle," she says. Adwoa snaps at her—"Sit still!"—then immediately feels a terrible guilt. She cannot explain that every time Ama moves the canoe, Adwoa sees her falling in, sees the net, sees the same surprise in her daughter's eyes. She has started checking the children's breathing while they sleep. She counts their ribs, their pulse. She cannot stop.

At the market, women ask about her catch. She smiles and says, "Small," but inside she is scanning the crowd for Kofi. She knows he is dead. She buried him. Yet sometimes she sees a man in a blue shirt from behind and her mouth goes dry, her chest tightens, and she walks toward him before catching herself. The world feels thin and treacherous, as if any moment the ground could tilt and swallow her whole. She drinks palm wine some evenings to quiet the roar in her head, but it only makes the mornings worse.

Her mother-in-law has begun to whisper that Adwoa is cursed, that she brought bad luck to the boat. Adwoa hears the murmurs but says nothing. She wonders the same thing. What did she do wrong? Why did she survive? She no longer prays at the shrine by the lake. She cannot bear to see the offerings of yams and coins left for a deity who let her husband drown.

The other fishermen try to be kind. They give her a portion of their catch sometimes. But they are careful around her, as if grief is contagious. Adwoa goes through each day mechanically: untangle the net, cast it, haul it, sell the fish, feed the children, lie down, wait for dawn. She does not cry. The tears feel locked behind a door that she is too tired to open. She only knows that the lake, once her life, is now a thing she must survive.
